claim: Automated extraction should move from one-shot generation toward context engineering, including retrieval, dynamic context assembly, tools, interaction, and memory.
limitation: Component evidence; integrated context-engineering workflow remains unvalidated.

claim: Accurate full-text retrieval and document conversion are foundational because digits, tables, and layout errors can distort downstream extraction.
limitation: Component evidence for preservation of source information.

claim: Directly processing long PDFs without retrieval or dynamic assembly may bury rare relevant evidence in large amounts of irrelevant text.
limitation: Component evidence; not proof that retrieval improves every extraction workflow.

claim: Some apparent LLM extraction errors may originate in opaque PDF parsing; small table or number parsing errors can cascade into major downstream errors.
limitation: Parsing and extraction are measurable separately; their causal error propagation requires a linked study.

claim: Tool calling or program-aided reasoning should let LLMs identify inputs while deterministic functions perform formal calculations.
limitation: Component evidence for numerical programs and tool calls; effect-size rule selection remains task-specific.

claim: Complex extraction requires intermediate steps, repeated retrieval, and regulated reasoning processes; chain-of-thought alone is not enough.
limitation: Component and indirect agent evidence; no claim that chain-of-thought alone solves extraction.

claim: The research agenda should explicitly address AI-induced bias, complacency, illusion of exploratory breadth, study quality, and AI methodology.
limitation: Several requirements, with substantial gaps for human attention, complacency and methodology.

claim: AI-induced bias may affect attention, search behavior, cross-checking, and decisions, even when AI only locates evidence.
limitation: Human interaction is only indirectly covered; source-based extraction reliance needs a direct experiment.

claim: AI can create an illusion of exploratory breadth when users believe the entire study knowledge set has been considered, although only AI-accessible material was processed.
limitation: Retrieval tests and interaction tests do not measure the proposed illusion of exhaustive coverage.

claim: Iterative prompt optimization will likely improve accuracy but may bias AI outputs toward the user's expectations.
limitation: Sycophancy tests are relevant to model response changes; iterative prompt-optimization bias in extraction is not directly tested.

claim: Iterative shaping may undermine the independence of an AI judge or AI second coder, especially under disagreement.
limitation: Valid-versus-invalid criticism is tested in component tasks; AI-judge independence under extraction disagreement remains open.

claim: Because meta-analyses influence theory, research, and policy, rigor must take priority over efficiency under speed-accuracy tradeoffs.
limitation: Normative priority; benchmark scores cannot establish the appropriate ethical balance between rigor and efficiency.

claim: Long-context capacity does not solve extraction automatically because LLMs may use information unevenly across the input.
limitation: Long-context component tasks directly operationalize uneven retrieval/retention, with task-specific conditions.

claim: The context-engineering examples are illustrative possibilities, not empirically validated performance evidence.
limitation: Status of the commentary examples; later component benchmarks do not retroactively validate those examples.

claim: LLM-based extraction raises legal and ethical issues around PDF parsing, RAG, derivative works, paywalled material, and commercial providers.
limitation: Legal and ethical requirements; no empirical capability benchmark can establish permission or compliance.

claim: LLM risk-of-bias accuracy varies strongly across domains and criteria; errors may come from wrong judgment or failed evidence location.
limitation: RoBBR separates methodological evidence and judgments in biomedical reports; transfer to other domains is limited.

claim: An occasional second coder will have less experience with the literature and may miss quirks, inconsistencies, and follow-up implications.
limitation: No benchmark here isolates occasional-coder experience or accumulated review-specific expertise.

claim: The original article is valuable because it establishes a psychology-specific benchmark across Psychological Bulletin reviews, variable types, and LLMs.
limitation: Historical characterization of the original study; it must be checked against that study, not a new general-purpose benchmark.

claim: Low accuracy for effect-size and numerical variables indicates that simple one-shot instruction-following is insufficient for complex psychology extraction.
limitation: Related numerical tasks motivate tests; the original agreement design cannot identify whether a human or LLM was wrong.

claim: TOPICS+M variables are easier than effect-size variables because effect-size extraction often requires symbolic induction, numerical derivation, and multiple source cues.
limitation: Component tasks distinguish numerical reasoning and binding, but do not independently explain the original variable-level discrepancies.

claim: Coding-protocol reproducibility is itself a source of error; missing codebooks and inferred variable meanings reduce accuracy.
limitation: Instruction/schema tasks assess explicit constraints; reconstruction of missing codebooks and construct validity remain unresolved.

claim: The original article shows impressive efficiency but inconsistent accuracy, creating a speed-accuracy tradeoff.
limitation: The original study measured agreement, not independently established human/model accuracy or a manipulated speed–accuracy trade-off.

claim: The AI role (assistant, independent second coder, judge) may affect deference and errors differently, especially when the role implies authority.
limitation: Existing interaction tasks are indirect for assistant/second-coder/judge roles in evidence extraction.

claim: Meta-analyst responsibility alone does not prevent algorithmic reliance; meaningful human control requires methods for detecting errors and omissions.
limitation: Error-detection tasks cover components; meaningful human control over the target workflow is not established.

claim: The original article found higher accuracy for LLM ensembles than single models, but this should be replicated across model sets.
limitation: A historical ensemble finding needs replication under a matched reference and model-set design; this register does not supply it.

claim: Several recommendations from the original article have not yet been empirically tested and should be evaluated before broad adoption.
limitation: Component evidence does not validate the original workflow recommendations as an integrated intervention.

claim: Bringing in a second human only for human-AI disagreements is efficient, but remains untested and depends on AI role and interaction design.
limitation: Disagreement-only human review has not been validated by these component tasks; shared errors also require auditing.

claim: A second human coder can serve as a noise ceiling for interpreting LLM performance under human error and protocol ambiguity.
limitation: A second human provides another judgment, not an infallible ceiling. No general human–LLM ranking follows from agreement.

claim: Risk-of-bias and study-quality assessment were outside the original article's target variables, but could become part of an expanded AI research agenda.
limitation: RoBBR is a directly relevant study-quality task, distinct from the variables in the original agreement study.
